reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Perforations arise most often from infection (acute or chronic otitis media) but also from trauma such as a slap to the ear, blast injury, barotrauma or instrumentation
Central perforations of the pars tensa are generally safe, whereas attic or marginal (posterosuperior) perforations are unsafe because they associate with cholesteatoma
The degree of conductive hearing loss reflects both the size and site of the perforation, being greater with larger and posterior defects
A discharging perforation suggests active middle ear disease and warrants aural toilet and treatment of infection
Many traumatic and small perforations heal spontaneously if the ear is kept dry and free of infection
Water precautions are important because contamination can precipitate recurrent infection and discharge
Persistent dry perforations affecting hearing or causing recurrent infection can be repaired by myringoplasty or tympanoplasty
Examination should assess the size, site and margins of the defect and the state of the middle ear mucosa and ossicles
reference.pathophysiology: The tympanic membrane can be breached when middle ear pressure rises from suppurative infection until necrosis of the drum produces a perforation, or when external forces (direct trauma, sudden pressure change, or a foreign body) tear it mechanically. Loss of an intact vibrating surface and of the round window sound-shielding effect reduces the efficiency of sound transfer to the cochlea, producing conductive hearing loss proportional to the area lost and its position. Small tears usually re-epithelialise and heal, but persistent perforation, ongoing infection, or ingrowth of squamous epithelium through a marginal or attic defect can prevent closure and predispose to cholesteatoma and chronic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Retracted but intact tympanic membrane simulating a defect
Healed thin (dimeric) segment mimicking a perforation
Cholesteatoma with a marginal or attic defect
Otitis externa with debris obscuring the drum
Congenital ossicular anomaly causing conductive loss with an intact drum
additionalInvestigations: Otoscopy and, ideally, microscopy to define size, site and margins of the perforation
Pure tone audiometry and tuning fork tests to quantify conductive loss
Tympanometry, which shows a large ear canal volume with a perforation
Culture of any discharge in active infection
CT of the temporal bone if cholesteatoma or ossicular pathology is suspected
redFlags: Marginal or attic perforation with foul discharge or crusting suggesting cholesteatoma
Vertigo, sensorineural loss or facial weakness indicating inner ear or facial nerve involvement
Perforation following head trauma with cerebrospinal fluid otorrhoea or associated fracture
Persistent bloody discharge or granulations raising concern for neoplasm
reference.prognosis: Small, uncomplicated and traumatic perforations often heal spontaneously with good recovery of hearing, and surgical repair of dry persistent defects has a high success rate; outcomes are worse when there is ongoing infection, ossicular damage or an underlying cholesteatoma.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish a dangerous marginal or attic perforation from a safe central one
Allowing water to enter the ear and precipitate recurrent infection
Assuming all perforations need surgery when many heal with conservative care
Overlooking ossicular discontinuity as an additional cause of hearing loss
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Watchful waiting with strict dry-ear precautions for small traumatic or infective perforations, most of which heal spontaneously
Treatment of active middle-ear infection with aural toilet and topical or systemic antibiotics, avoiding potentially ototoxic drops reaching the middle ear
Water precautions to prevent contamination and recurrent discharge
Surgical repair by myringoplasty or tympanoplasty for persistent dry perforations, with ossicular reconstruction where required
Urgent otological assessment and temporal-bone CT for marginal or attic (unsafe) perforations given the risk of cholesteatoma
Audiometric assessment and hearing rehabilitation for conductive hearing loss
ENT referral for non-healing, discharging or complicated perforations
